item.title: Anatomy of an EIT Reconstruction
item.description: An iterative EIT reconstruction repeatedly compares simulated with measured data and improves the conductivity. It combines five exchangeable pieces.

item.title: Choosing a Linear Solver
item.description: The systems A(\sigma)X = B of EIT are sparse, symmetric and positive semidefinite.

item.title: Choosing an Optimizer
item.description: Which method minimises J(\sigma) = \Phi(\sigma)+\alpha R(\sigma) best depends mainly on two properties: whether the misfit \Phi is a sum of squares, and whether the regulariser R is smooth.

item.title: Classical and Learned Priors
item.description: Because EIT is severely ill-posed (see Stability of the Calderón Problem), prior knowledge about the conductivity determines what a reconstruction can show.

item.title: From Physics to Linear Algebra
item.description: EIT starts with Maxwell’s equations and ends, in the computer, with sparse symmetric linear systems.

item.title: Overviews
item.description: Short articles that connect the topics of the wiki. Each follows one thread through several chapters and links to the detailed articles along the way.

item.title: Applications of EIT
item.description: Electrical Impedance Tomography is used wherever conductivity contrasts show up and a cheap, fast, non-invasive measurement matters more than fine spatial resolution.

item.title: Complete Electrode Model
item.description: The Complete Electrode Model (CEM) is the standard forward model for real EIT measurements (see Electrode Models).

item.title: Complex Conductivity
item.description: Biological tissue both conducts and stores charge: cell membranes act as capacitors.
